verses.translation: And when he opened{H6605} the seventh{H7637}, all of them{H3605} fell silent{H8367} in the heavens{H8064} for about one hour.

one_way_hebrew: Uses Aramaic חֲדָא (chada — 'one') instead of Hebrew אֶחָד/אַחַת (echad/achat). This is a bilingual marker — a Hebrew author naturally code-switching into Aramaic, as first-century Jews did daily. A back-translator from Greek ἡμιώριον ('half an hour') would use the standard Hebrew אחת, not an Aramaic numeral. The casual mixing of Hebrew and Aramaic is a hallmark of authentic first-century Jewish composition.

Uses כֵּיוָן (keivan — 'when/as soon as') — a post-biblical Hebrew conjunction from Aramaic. Biblical Hebrew would use כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka'asher). No back-translator from Greek ὅτε ('when') would produce this distinctively later Hebrew/Aramaic form.

Uses שׁוֹתְקִים (shotkím — active participle, 'were being silent', H8367) — all of them actively silenced themselves. Greek σιγή (sige) is a noun ('silence') — a passive state. The Hebrew depicts persons choosing to be silent; the Greek merely reports that silence existed. A back-translator from the Greek noun would use a nominal construction like דממה (demamah — 'stillness'), not the active participle of שתק.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'about one hour' (כְּשָׁעָה חֲדָא). Greek: 'about half an hour' (ὡς ἡμιώριον). The Hebrew has a full hour; the Greek has half.
Hebrew: 'the seventh' — no object specified, relying on context. Greek: 'the seventh seal' (τὴν σφραγῖδα τὴν ἑβδόμην) — makes the referent explicit.
translation_notes: The Hebrew omits 'seal' (חותם) after 'the seventh,' relying on the reader to follow from the preceding chapter. This economy of expression is characteristic of Hebrew narrative style.
textual_notes: The mixing of Hebrew and Aramaic (כיון, חדא) alongside standard Hebrew forms places this text in the linguistic world of first-century Jewish Palestine, where both languages were in daily use. This is natural for a native author but implausible for a back-translator working from a single-language Greek source.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} coming{H935} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}, and to them were given{H5414} seven{H7651} ram's horns{H7782}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shopharot — 'ram's horns', H7782) — the specific curved horn of a ram, blown in Torah ceremonies (Lev 25:9), at Sinai (Ex 19:16,19), and at Jericho (Josh 6:4-20). Greek uses σάλπιγγες (salpinges — 'trumpets'), a generic term for metal instruments. A back-translator from Greek would use חֲצוֹצְרוֹת (chatsotsrot — 'trumpets', Num 10:2) — the Hebrew word for the silver trumpets. No one translating σάλπιγξ would choose שׁוֹפָר, the ram's horn of the covenant. This single word choice connects the seven blasts to Jericho, to Sinai, and to Yom Kippur. The Hebrew author writes shopharot throughout this chapter (vv.2,6,13) — never trumpets.

Uses בָּאִים (ba'im — 'coming', active participle of H935) — the messengers are arriving in procession before YHWH. Greek has ἑστήκασι ('have stood/stand' — perfect of ἵστημι), depicting them already stationed. The Hebrew presents a dynamic scene of approach; the Greek presents a static tableau. A back-translator from Greek would use עוֹמְדִים (omdim — 'standing'), not באים.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: לִפְנֵי יַהְוֶה ('before YHWH'). Greek: ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ ('before God'). The Hebrew uses the personal covenant name; the Greek uses the generic title. This pattern recurs throughout the chapter (vv.2,4).
Hebrew: 'coming before' (באים). Greek: 'standing before' (ἑστήκασι). Different postures — procession vs. station.
translation_notes: 'Ram's horns' for shopharot — the shofar is specifically the curved horn of a ram (or ibex), not a manufactured metal instrument. The seven shopharot echo the seven ram's horns of Jericho (Josh 6:4: שִׁבְעָה שׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּוֹבְלִים — 'seven ram's horns of jubilee').
textual_notes: The seven-shofar pattern is established in Joshua 6:4 — seven priests with seven shopharot circle Jericho for seven days. In Revelation 8, seven messengers with seven shopharot unleash judgment. The Hebrew connects these events through identical vocabulary.

verses.translation: And another{H312} messenger{H4397} came{H935} and trod{H1869} beside{H681} the sanctuary{H1964}, and in his hand{H3027} were fire-pans{H4289} of gold{H2091}; and to him was given{H5414} much incense{H7004} to place for the prayer{H8605} of the holy ones{H6918}, before{H6440} the sanctuary{H1964} and before{H6440} the throne{H3678}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans', PLURAL, H4289) — the specific vessels for carrying live coals in the Tabernacle/Temple service. This is the exact word for the fire-pan in Leviticus 16:12 (Yom Kippur: 'he shall take a fire-pan full of coals of fire'), Numbers 16:6,17,37-39 (Korah's rebellion), and Exodus 27:3. Greek has λιβανωτόν (libanōton — 'censer', SINGULAR). A back-translator from Greek would use מַקְטֶרֶת (maqteret — 'incense burner') or transliterate, not reach for the Levitical fire-pan word. The PLURAL also matters — in v5 the text switches to singular הַמַּחְתָּה ('THE fire-pan'), suggesting the messenger selects one from a set, mirroring Temple ritual procedure.

Uses דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod/marched', H1869) — a verb meaning to step purposefully, used for treading a winepress (Isa 63:3), drawing a bow (Ps 7:13), and marching in military procession. Greek has ἐστάθη ('stood'). A back-translator from Greek would use עָמַד (amad — 'stood'), not the dynamic דרך. The Hebrew presents the messenger treading with purpose toward the sanctuary — a priestly/military approach, not a static posture.

Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal — 'sanctuary/temple', H1964) — the specific word for the Temple's inner hall, Solomon's sanctuary (1 Ki 6:3,5,17), and the heavenly sanctuary (Ps 11:4, 18:7). Greek has θυσιαστήριον ('altar'). The Hebrew locates the messenger at the sanctuary building; the Greek locates him at the altar. A back-translator from Greek 'altar' would use מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach), not heikhal.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trod beside the sanctuary' (דרך אצל ההיכל). Greek: 'stood upon the altar' (ἐστάθη ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον). Different verb, different preposition, different location.
Hebrew: מחתות (PLURAL, 'fire-pans'). Greek: λιβανωτόν (SINGULAR, 'censer'). Different number and different vessel type.
Hebrew: 'before the sanctuary and before the throne' — two locations. Greek: 'upon the golden altar before the throne' — one location (the altar).
Greek adds 'all' (πάντων) to 'the prayers of ALL the saints' — absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Fire-pans' for machtot — preserving the Levitical vessel type. These are the flat, shovel-like pans used to carry live coals, not enclosed censers.
'Trod' for darakh — capturing the purposeful, weighty step of priestly approach. The messenger doesn't merely 'stand' — he treads with authority.

The entire scene mirrors the Yom Kippur service of Leviticus 16:12-13 — the High Priest takes the fire-pan of coals, adds incense, and brings the cloud of incense before the mercy seat. The Hebrew vocabulary (machtah, qetoret, heikhal) is identical to the Torah's Yom Kippur instructions.
textual_notes: Leviticus 16:12-13: 'He shall take a fire-pan (מַחְתָּה) full of coals of fire from upon the altar before YHWH, and two handfuls of finely ground incense (קְטֹרֶת), and bring it inside the curtain.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this Yom Kippur scene — fire-pan, incense, and approach to the divine presence.

verses.translation: And the smoke{H6227} from the incense{H7004} of the holy ones{H6918} went{H1980} from the hand{H3027} of the messenger{H4397} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went/walked', H1980) for the smoke's movement. Greek has ἀνέβη (anebe — 'ascended'). A back-translator from Greek 'ascended' would use עָלָה (alah — 'went up'), not the general movement verb הלך. The Hebrew doesn't impose upward direction — the smoke simply 'went' before YHWH. The Greek assumes vertical ascent; the Hebrew describes horizontal/general movement toward the divine presence.

The phrase קְטֹרֶת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('incense OF the holy ones') treats the incense as BELONGING TO the holy ones — it is their incense, their offering. Greek has θυμιαμάτων ταῖς προσευχαῖς τῶν ἁγίων ('incense WITH the prayers of the saints') — incense and prayers as two separate things traveling together. The Hebrew IDENTIFIES incense with the holy ones' offering; the Greek ACCOMPANIES prayer with incense. This echoes Psalm 141:2: 'Let my prayer be set before you as incense' (תִּכּוֹן תְּפִלָּתִי קְטֹרֶת לְפָנֶיךָ).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הלך ('went'). Greek: ἀνέβη ('ascended'). Different directional concepts.
Hebrew: 'incense of the holy ones' (genitive possession). Greek: 'incense with/to the prayers of the saints' (dative association). Different grammatical relationship between incense and the saints.
translation_notes: 'Went' for halakh — preserving the Hebrew's non-directional description. The smoke 'went' before YHWH without specifying upward motion.
textual_notes: Psalm 141:2 provides the conceptual key: prayer IS incense before YHWH. The Hebrew construction 'incense of the holy ones' embodies this identification — the incense represents them directly.

verses.translation: And the messenger{H4397} took{H3947} the fire-pan{H4289} and filled{H4390} it with fire{H784} and poured it out{H3332} upon the earth{H776}; and there came thunderings{H6963} and thunders{H7482} and lightnings{H1300}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יָצַק (yatsaq — 'poured out', H3332) — the specific verb for pouring molten metal (Ex 25:12, 1 Ki 7:24), pouring oil (2 Ki 4:4), and pouring libations. This is a deliberate, controlled, priestly/liturgical action. Greek has ἔβαλεν (ebalen — 'cast/threw'). A back-translator from Greek 'threw' would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'cast/threw'), not the liturgical pouring verb. The Hebrew presents the fire-casting as a sacred ritual act — a priestly pouring; the Greek presents it as a violent throw.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'thunderings/voices', H6963) — the SAME word used in Exodus 9:23,28,29,33,34 for the 'thunderings' that accompanied the seventh plague of hail and fire. The next verse (v7) describes hail and fire falling on earth. The Hebrew author uses the Exodus plague vocabulary as a deliberate setup for the plague sequence that follows. Greek φωναί ('voices') is generic.

Note the switch from PLURAL מַחְתּוֹת ('fire-pans', v3) to SINGULAR הַמַּחְתָּה ('THE fire-pan', v5). The messenger arrived carrying multiple fire-pans but selects THE specific one for the ritual — mirroring Temple procedure where multiple vessels existed but specific ones were designated for specific rites.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יצק ('poured' — controlled, ritual). Greek: ἔβαλεν ('threw/cast' — abrupt, forceful). Different types of action.
Hebrew: 'filled it with fire' (no source specified). Greek: 'filled it from the fire of the altar' (ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου). Greek adds 'of the altar' as the fire's source.
Greek adds σεισμός ('earthquake') after thunders and lightnings — entirely absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew has only three phenomena (thunderings, thunders, lightnings); the Greek has four.
translation_notes: 'Poured out' for yatsaq captures the liturgical precision — not a violent throw but a deliberate ritual pouring of sacred fire upon the earth.

'Thunderings' for qolot — this word means both 'voices' and 'thunderclaps.' In the Exodus plague context, it specifically denotes thunder (Ex 9:23). The translation 'thunderings' preserves the Exodus connection.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:23 — 'YHWH sent thunderings (קֹלֹת) and hail, and fire ran down to the earth.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this sequence: qolot first, then (in v7) hail and fire upon the earth. The Exodus plague framework is unmistakable.

verses.translation: And the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} with the seven{H7651} ram's horns{H7782} were prepared{H3559} to blast{H8628}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לִתְקוֹעַ (litqoa — 'to blast', infinitive of H8628) — the specific verb for blowing the shofar throughout the OT. תקע is the technical term in Joshua 6:4,9,13,16,20 for the shofar blasts at Jericho, in Numbers 10:3-10 for the shofar signals of the camp, and in Joel 2:1,15 for the alarm shofar. Greek σαλπίσωσι (salpisōsi) is a generic verb for any instrument. A back-translator from the generic Greek verb would not produce this shofar-specific Hebrew term. The verb תקע and the noun שׁוֹפָר form a fixed Hebrew pair — they belong together in a way that no Greek vocabulary can replicate.

Uses מוּכָנִים (muchanim — 'prepared/readied', from kun H3559 — 'to be established/prepared'). This is the same root used in Exodus 19:11,15 when Israel was told to be 'prepared' (נְכֹנִים) for the Sinai theophany. The messengers are 'prepared' for the shofar blasts using the same vocabulary Israel was 'prepared' for the revelation at Sinai — the first time God spoke amid shofar blasts (Ex 19:16,19). A back-translator from Greek ἡτοίμασαν ('prepared themselves') could use הכינו (hechinu) but would miss the Sinai-theophany resonance that a Hebrew author naturally produces.
translation_notes: 'Blast' for תקע — this is a sharp, penetrating sound produced by the ram's horn, not a melodic trumpet call. The Hebrew תקיעה (teqi'ah) remains the technical term for the shofar blast in Jewish liturgy to this day.
'Prepared' for muchanim echoes the Sinai preparation — Israel readied itself for divine encounter, and now the messengers ready themselves for divine judgment.
textual_notes: Joshua 6:4 — 'seven priests shall carry seven ram's horns of jubilee (שִׁבְעָה שׁוֹפְרוֹת הַיּוֹבְלִים) before the ark.' Seven shopharot, seven priests, seven days. Revelation 8 mirrors this: seven shopharot, seven messengers, seven judgments.

verses.translation: And the first{H7223} messenger{H4397} blasted{H8628}, and there was hail{H1259} and fire{H784} mixed{H1101} with blood{H1818}; and it fell{H5307} upon the earth{H776}, and a third of the trees{H6086} was burned{H8313}, and all{H3605} the green herbage{H3418} of the field{H7704} was burned{H8313}.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 7TH PLAGUE: The entire verse reproduces the seventh plague of Egypt — hail and fire (Exodus 9:23-24: 'YHWH sent thunderings and hail, and fire ran down to the earth'). The Hebrew vocabulary directly parallels the Exodus account: ברד (hail), אשׁ (fire), ארץ (earth). The preceding verse's קולות ('thunderings') completes the Exodus 9:23 tableau.

Uses בָּלֻל (balul — 'mixed', pual passive of H1101) — the specific verb for MIXING grain offerings with oil in Torah sacrifices (Lev 2:4-5, 7:10,12; Ex 29:2: חַלֹּת מַצּוֹת בְּלוּלֹת בַּשֶּׁמֶן — 'unleavened cakes mixed with oil'). The hail and fire are described as 'mixed' (balul) using OFFERING vocabulary — as if the judgment is itself a sacrifice. Greek μεμιγμένα (memigmena) is generic 'mixed.' This same root בלל (balal) gives Babel its name (Gen 11:9 — 'he confused/mixed'). A back-translator from Greek would use מעורב (me'orav — 'mixed'), not the sacrificial/Babel-laden בלול.

Uses יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה ('green herbage of the field', H3418 + H7704) — echoing Exodus 10:15 where the locusts ate 'every green thing' (כָּל יֶרֶק), and Genesis 1:30 ('every green herb'). Greek has πᾶς χόρτος χλωρός ('all green grass'). The Hebrew adds הַשָּׂדֶה ('of the field') which is absent from Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write כל עשב ירוק ('all green grass'), not the OT-rooted ירק השדה. The phrase connects this destruction to the creation and plague narratives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: ירק השדה ('green herbage of the field'). Greek: πᾶς χόρτος χλωρός ('all green grass'). Different botanical terms; Hebrew adds 'of the field.'
Hebrew uses בלול ('mixed' — sacrificial/Babel vocabulary). Greek uses μεμιγμένα ('mixed' — generic).
translation_notes: 'Mixed' for balul preserves the sacrificial offering resonance. The hail-fire-blood mixture is described using the same verb as grain offerings mixed with oil.
'Green herbage of the field' for yereq hasadeh — this is broader than 'grass'; yereq encompasses all green vegetation, connecting to Genesis 1's creation of plant life.
textual_notes: Exodus 9:23-25: 'YHWH sent thunderings (קלת) and hail (ברד), and fire (אשׁ) ran down to the earth (ארצה)... and the hail struck every herb of the field (כל עשב השדה) and broke every tree of the field (כל עץ השדה).' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces this plague with its Torah vocabulary intact: hail, fire, trees, green herbage of the field.

verses.translation: And the second{H8145} blasted{H8628}, and there was something like a great{H1419} mountain{H2022} burning{H8313} with fire{H784}, and it went{H1980} into the sea{H3220}; and a third of the sea{H3220} became blood{H1818}.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 1ST PLAGUE: Water turned to blood (Ex 7:20-21: 'all the water in the river was turned to blood'). The Hebrew naturally connects sea-to-blood with the Nile-to-blood plague. The Hebrew language of 'became blood' (היה דם) echoes the Exodus phrasing.

Uses הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went', H1980) — the burning mountain WENT into the sea under its own power or by divine propulsion. Greek has ἐβλήθη (eblethe — 'was thrown/cast'), a passive verb implying an external agent threw it. A back-translator from Greek 'was thrown' would use הֻשְׁלַךְ (hushlakh — 'was cast'), not the active movement verb הלך. The Hebrew presents the mountain as moving with agency — walking, going — while the Greek presents it as passively thrown. This is a fundamental difference in how the event is conceived.

The consonantal text שרף (soref — 'burning') resonates with שרפים (seraphim — 'burning ones', Isa 6:2,6). While the pointed text reads as a participle meaning 'burning,' the consonantal ambiguity with 'seraph' may be intentional — a great mountain, a fiery being, going into the sea.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: הלך ('went' — active, self-directed motion). Greek: ἐβλήθη ('was thrown' — passive). Fundamentally different agency.
Greek adds ὡς λαμπάς ('like a torch') — absent from the Hebrew's simpler description.
translation_notes: 'Went' for halakh — preserving the Hebrew's depiction of active movement, not passive casting.

Jeremiah 51:25 provides an OT precedent: 'Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain (הר המשחית)... I will make you a burned mountain (הר שרפה).' The image of a burning mountain cast into judgment has prophetic roots.
textual_notes: The sea turning to blood combines two Exodus motifs: the first plague (Nile→blood, Ex 7:20) and the Red Sea judgment. The Hebrew author layers these plague memories.

verses.translation: And a third of the creations of the sea{H3220} died{H4191}, and a third of the ships{H5600} were sunk{H2883}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נִטְבְּעוּ (nitbe'u — 'were sunk', nifal of tava H2883) — the EXACT verb used for the Egyptians sinking in the Red Sea. Exodus 15:4: טֻבְּעוּ בְיַם סוּף ('they were sunk in the Sea of Reeds'). The ships are described as 'sinking' using the Red Sea victory vocabulary. Greek has διεφθάρη (diephthare — 'were destroyed/corrupted'). A back-translator from Greek 'destroyed' would use נִשְׁחֲתוּ (nishchatu — 'were corrupted/destroyed'), NOT the Red Sea sinking verb. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter — the Hebrew author instinctively uses Exodus vocabulary for maritime catastrophe.

Uses בְּרִיאוֹת (bri'ot — 'creations', from bara H1254 — 'to create') — the sea creatures are called 'creations,' using the root exclusively reserved for divine creation in the OT (Gen 1:1,21,27; 2:3,4; 5:1,2). Greek has κτισμάτων (ktismaton — 'created things'), which is conceptually parallel but uses a different root. The Hebrew connects the sea creatures directly to Genesis 1:21 where God 'created (ברא) the great sea creatures.' The destruction undoes the creation.

Uses סְפִינוֹת (sefinot — 'ships', H5600) — the authentic Hebrew word for sea-going vessels, used in Jonah 1:5 (the prophet descending into the hold of the סְפִינָה). Greek uses πλοίων (ploiōn — 'boats'). The Hebrew word is rarer and more literary than the common אֳנִיָּה (oniyyah — 'ship').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: ניטבעים ('were sunk' — Red Sea vocabulary). Greek: διεφθάρη ('were destroyed'). Entirely different verbs with different echoes.
Hebrew: בריאות ('creations'). Greek adds τὰ ἔχοντα ψυχάς ('having souls/lives') — a qualifier absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Creations' for bri'ot — preserving the Genesis creation verb ברא. These are not merely 'creatures' but divine creations being destroyed.
'Sunk' for nitba'im — the Red Sea echo is essential. The ships sink as Pharaoh's army sank.
textual_notes: Exodus 15:4-5 (Song of the Sea): 'Pharaoh's chariots and his army he cast into the sea... they sank (טֻבְּעוּ) in the Sea of Reeds. The depths covered them; they went down (ירדו) into the depths like a stone.' The Hebrew Revelation uses this exact verb for the ships' fate, linking the second shofar judgment to the Red Sea.

verses.translation: And the third{H7992} blasted{H8628}, and one{H259} star{H3556} fell{H5307} from the heavens{H8064}, burning{H8313}, and it fell{H5307} upon a third of the wells{H875} of water{H4325}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּאֵרוֹת (be'erot — 'wells/springs', plural of be'er H875). Greek has ποταμῶν ('rivers') and πηγάς ('springs'). A back-translator from Greek 'rivers' would use נְהָרוֹת (neharot — 'rivers'), NOT the patriarchal well vocabulary. Wells (be'erot) are foundational to Hebrew identity — Beer-sheba (Gen 21:31), Beer-lahai-roi (Gen 16:14), the well disputes of Isaac (Gen 26:15-22), the well where Jacob met Rachel (Gen 29:2-10). The Hebrew author sees water sources as 'wells' — the communal gathering places of Israel's ancestors. The Greek author sees them as 'rivers.' These are different cultural frames that a back-translator would never interchange.

Hebrew describes the star as כוכב אחד ('one star' — H259). Greek has ἀστὴρ μέγας ('a great star'). The Hebrew emphasizes its singularity ('one'); the Greek emphasizes its size ('great'). A back-translator from Greek would write כוכב גדול ('a great star'), not כוכב אחד ('one star').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: בארות ('wells'). Greek: ποταμῶν καὶ πηγάς ('rivers and springs'). Different water sources — Hebrew has ONE type (wells); Greek has TWO types (rivers and springs).
Hebrew: כוכב אחד ('one star'). Greek: ἀστὴρ μέγας ('a great star'). Different attribute — singularity vs. magnitude.
Greek adds ὡς λαμπάς ('like a torch') — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot — NOT 'rivers.' The Hebrew locates the contamination at the communal water sources central to Israelite life. Wells are where communities gather, where marriages are arranged, where covenants are made.
textual_notes: The poisoning of wells connects to Exodus 15:23 (the bitter waters of Marah) which the next verse will develop. It also evokes the well-poisoning motif — the destruction of what sustains communal life.

verses.translation: And the name{H8034} of the star{H3556} was Worm{H8438}; and a third of the waters{H4325} became bitter{H4751}, and many sons of{H1121} adam{H120} died{H4191} by the hand{H3027} of the waters{H4325}, because of their embitterers{H4843}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תּוֹלַעַת (tola'at — 'worm', H8438) as the star's name. Greek uses Ἄψινθος (Apsinthos — 'Wormwood,' the bitter plant). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write לַעֲנָה (la'anah — 'wormwood', H3939), the standard Hebrew word for the bitter plant (Deut 29:17, Jer 9:14, 23:15, Amos 5:7). No back-translator would render 'Wormwood' as 'Worm.' The Hebrew תולעת carries completely different associations: the scarlet worm (תּוֹלַעַת שָׁנִי) used for Tabernacle dye (Ex 25:4, 26:1, 28:5), the worm of decay (Isa 14:11, 41:14, 66:24 — 'their worm shall not die'), and Psalm 22:7 — 'I am a worm (תולעת) and not a man.' The star is named 'Worm' — decay, corruption, mortality — not after a plant.

Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם (bene adam — 'sons of adam/man', H1121 + H120) — the Genesis creation term, emphasizing humanity as descendants of the original adam formed from adamah. Greek has ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn — 'men', generic). A back-translator from Greek would write אנשׁים (anashim — 'men') or simply אדם ('men'), not the compound form בני אדם which carries the Genesis genealogical weight.

Uses עַל יַד הַמַּיִם ('by the hand of the waters') — the idiom על יד (al yad, 'upon the hand of') personifies the waters as having agency, as if they acted with hands. This idiom is used in the OT for acting through agents: 'by the hand of Moses' (ביד משה), 'by the hand of YHWH' (ביד יהוה). Greek simply says ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων ('from the waters') — no personification. A back-translator would use מן המים ('from the waters'), not the personifying idiom.

MARAH PARALLEL: The waters 'became bitter' (היה מר) — directly echoing Exodus 15:23: 'they could not drink the waters of Marah, for they were bitter (מָרִים); therefore its name was called Marah (מָרָה).' The third Exodus plague-echo in sequence.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: תולעת ('Worm'). Greek: Ἄψινθος ('Wormwood' — a plant). Entirely different names with different semantic fields: worm (decay/mortality) vs. wormwood (bitterness).
Hebrew: בני אדם ('sons of adam'). Greek: ἀνθρώπων ('men'). Different anthropological framing.
Hebrew: על יד המים ('by the hand of the waters'). Greek: ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων ('from the waters'). Hebrew personifies; Greek does not.

Hebrew: מפני מורריהם ('because of their embitterers'). Greek: ὅτι ἐπικράνθησαν ('because they were embittered'). Hebrew uses an active agentive noun ('embitterers'); Greek uses a passive verb ('were embittered').
translation_notes: 'Worm' for tola'at — NOT 'wormwood.' The Hebrew name invokes decay and mortality, not merely bitterness. The worm that devours in the grave (Isa 14:11) and the scarlet-worm of the Tabernacle (Ex 25:4) share this word.
'Sons of adam' — preserving the creation genealogy. Humanity dies 'by the hand of the waters' as descendants of the adam who was formed from the ground.
'Embitterers' for morrereihem — a rare agentive form from the root מרר (to be bitter), suggesting active agents of bitterness within the waters.
textual_notes: Exodus 15:23-25: 'When they came to Marah, they could not drink the waters... for they were bitter (מרים)... and YHWH showed him a tree, and he cast it into the waters, and the waters became sweet.' At Marah, a tree made bitter water sweet; in Revelation, a falling star (Worm) makes sweet water bitter — an inverted Exodus. The Hebrew vocabulary (מר, מים) is identical.
Isaiah 14:11 — 'the worm (תולעת) is spread under you' — spoken to the king of Babylon cast down from heaven. A star named 'Worm' falling from heaven echoes this Isaiah imagery of a fallen ruler.

verses.translation: And the fourth{H7243} blasted{H8628}, and a third of the sun{H8121} and the moon{H3394} and the stars{H3556} was eclipsed, and a third of the day{H3117} did not shine{H2224}, and also{H1571} the night{H3915}.

one_way_hebrew: EXODUS 9TH PLAGUE: Darkness (Exodus 10:21-23 — 'there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days'). The fourth plague-echo in sequence: hail/fire (7th plague), blood (1st plague), bitter water (Marah), now darkness (9th plague). The Hebrew author follows the Exodus plague framework.

Uses נִלְקָה (nilqah — 'was eclipsed') — a technical astronomical term in Hebrew. The root לקה in later Hebrew specifically means 'to be eclipsed' (ליקוי חמה = 'solar eclipse'; ליקוי לבנה = 'lunar eclipse'). This is specialist vocabulary that a Hebrew astronomer/author would naturally use. Greek has ἐπλήγη ('was struck') — a generic verb. A back-translator from Greek would use הֻכָּה (hukah — 'was struck'), not the technical astronomical term for eclipse. This word choice reveals an author thinking in Hebrew astronomical categories.

Uses זֹרֵחַ (zoreach — 'shining/rising', qal participle of zarach H2224) — the specific Hebrew verb for the rising/shining of the sun (Gen 32:32, Judg 9:33, 2 Sam 23:4). Malachi 3:20 [4:2]: 'the sun of righteousness shall rise (זרח) with healing in its wings.' Greek has φαίνω ('shine/appear') — generic. A back-translator would use מאיר (me'ir — 'giving light') or simply אור ('light'), not the sunrise-specific verb zarach.

MANUSCRIPT LACUNA: The text contains [   ] — a gap between נלקה and השלישׁ, indicating a word was illegible or missing in the source manuscript. This physical manuscript artifact would not exist in a back-translation from Greek, which would flow without gaps. This is evidence of copying from an actual Hebrew manuscript.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נלקה ('was eclipsed' — technical astronomical term). Greek: ἐπλήγη ('was struck' — generic).
Hebrew: לא זורח ('not shining/rising'). Greek: μὴ φαίνῃ ('not appearing/shining'). Different verbs — Hebrew uses the sunrise verb.
Hebrew has a manuscript lacuna [   ] — absent from Greek, which flows continuously.
translation_notes: 'Eclipsed' for nilqah — this is the precise Hebrew astronomical term, not merely 'struck' or 'smitten.' The luminaries undergo eclipse, not assault.
'Shine' for zoreach — this verb specifically denotes the rising/radiating of the sun. The day 'does not zarach' — the sunrise itself fails.
textual_notes: Exodus 10:21-22: 'YHWH said to Moses, Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt... and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.' The fourth shofar judgment echoes this ninth plague. Note: in Exodus, darkness is the plague before the final devastating plague (death of firstborn). In Revelation, darkness (v12) precedes the three 'woes' announced in v13.
Joel 2:31 [3:4]: 'The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and terrible day of YHWH comes.' The eclipse of luminaries is a standard Hebrew prophetic sign.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} and heard{H8085} one{H259} messenger{H4397} hovering{H7363} in the heavens{H8064}, and he cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}: Woe{H188}, woe{H188}, woe{H188} to those who dwell upon the earth{H776}, because of the sound{H6963} of the ram's horns{H7782} that the three{H7969} messengers{H4397} must yet{H5750} blast{H8628}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רֹחֵף (rochef — 'hovering', H7363) — the EXACT verb from Genesis 1:2 where the Spirit of God 'hovered' (מְרַחֶפֶת) over the face of the waters. This verb occurs only TWICE in the entire OT: Genesis 1:2 (the Spirit hovering over creation) and Deuteronomy 32:11 (an eagle hovering over its young). Greek has πετωμένου (petōmenou — 'flying'). A back-translator from Greek would use עָף (af — 'flying', H5774), the common Hebrew word for flight. No one translating 'flying' would reach for the exceedingly rare creation-verb רחף. The messenger 'hovers' in the heavens using the same verb as the Spirit at creation — the undoing of creation (plagues on earth, sea, water, sky) is witnessed by one who hovers as the Spirit once hovered over the primordial deep.

Uses צָעַק (tsa'aq — 'cried out', H6817) — a verb of distress, urgent outcry, and prophetic alarm (Ex 14:10, Judg 3:9, 1 Sam 7:9, Isa 19:20). This is the cry of Israel in Egypt (Ex 14:10), the cry of the oppressed seeking deliverance. Greek has λέγοντος ('saying') — neutral speech. A back-translator from Greek 'saying' would use אמר (amar — 'said'), not the anguished outcry verb צעק.

Uses הַשּׁוֹפָרֹת (hashopharot — 'the ram's horns', H7782) a final time, maintaining the shofar vocabulary throughout the chapter. Greek σάλπιγγος ('trumpet') never captures the shofar's covenantal significance. The Hebrew 'sound of the shopharot' (קול השופרות) is a fixed biblical phrase (Josh 6:5,20; 2 Sam 6:15; Ps 47:6).

NOTE: Some Greek manuscripts read ἀετοῦ ('eagle') instead of ἀγγέλου ('angel'). If the original Greek had 'eagle,' then the Hebrew verb רחף is even more striking — Deuteronomy 32:11 uses רחף SPECIFICALLY for an eagle hovering over its young. The Hebrew verb choice perfectly matches the eagle tradition that some Greek manuscripts preserve, suggesting the Hebrew is closer to the original reading.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רחף ('hovering' — Genesis 1:2 creation verb). Greek: πετωμένου ('flying' — generic). Fundamentally different verbs.
Hebrew: בשמים ('in the heavens'). Greek: ἐν μεσουρανήματι ('in mid-heaven'). Different spatial descriptions.
Hebrew: צעק ('cried out' — distress cry). Greek: λέγοντος ('saying' — neutral speech).
Hebrew: שצריכים ('that must' — later Hebrew necessity word). Greek: τῶν μελλόντων ('who are about to'). Different modality — Hebrew expresses obligation; Greek expresses imminence.
translation_notes: 'Hovering' for rochef — this is the Genesis 1:2 creation verb, NOT mere 'flying.' The messenger hovers over the earth as the Spirit once hovered over the waters.
'Cried out' for tsa'aq — capturing the prophetic distress. This is not calm speech but an anguished warning cry.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') and צְרִיכִים (tsrikhim — 'must/need') are later Hebrew forms without standard Strong's numbers, characteristic of the text's first-century linguistic layer.
הַדָּרִים (hadarim — 'the dwellers') is from a later Hebrew form meaning 'residents/inhabitants.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2: וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם — 'and the Spirit of Elohim was hovering over the face of the waters.' Deuteronomy 32:11: כְּנֶשֶׁר יָעִיר קִנּוֹ עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף — 'like an eagle stirs up its nest, over its young it hovers.' These are the ONLY two OT occurrences of רחף. A messenger using this verb in the heavens invokes both the Spirit at creation and the protective eagle of Deuteronomy's Song of Moses.

The three woes (אוי אוי אוי) correspond to the three remaining shofar blasts. The structure parallels Ezekiel 16:23 (וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי כָּל רָעָתֵךְ אוֹי אוֹי לָךְ — 'woe, woe to you') and Isaiah 6:3's triple-holy (קדושׁ קדושׁ קדושׁ) — three-fold repetition for emphasis and completeness.

chapter_notes.summary:
Revelation 8 in Hebrew is structured as a three-part liturgical drama: (1) the Yom Kippur ceremony (vv.3-5), (2) the Exodus plague sequence (vv.7-12), and (3) the Jericho shofar pattern (throughout). The Hebrew vocabulary consistently uses Torah/Temple terminology that the Greek cannot capture.

The chapter contains at least 15 strong one-way translation markers:

1. שׁוֹפָרוֹת (shopharot — 'ram's horns') vs Greek σάλπιγγες ('trumpets') — used three times (vv.2,6,13), connecting to Jericho (Josh 6), Sinai (Ex 19), and Yom Kippur (Lev 25:9).
2. מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans') — Levitical fire-pan vocabulary (Lev 16:12, Num 16:6) vs Greek λιβανωτόν ('censer').
3. תְּקִיעָה vocabulary: לִתְקוֹעַ/תּוֹקֵעַ (to blast) — the shofar-specific verb vs generic Greek σαλπίζω.
4. דָּרַךְ (darakh — 'trod') vs Greek ἐστάθη ('stood') — dynamic priestly approach vs static posture.
5. יָצַק (yatsaq — 'poured') vs Greek ἔβαλεν ('threw') — liturgical pouring vs violent casting.
6. בָּלוּל (balul — 'mixed') — Torah offering/Babel vocabulary vs generic Greek μεμιγμένα.
7. יֶרֶק הַשָּׂדֶה ('green herbage of the field') — Exodus plague vegetation vs Greek χόρτος ('grass').
8. הָלַךְ (halakh — 'went') for the burning mountain vs Greek ἐβλήθη ('was thrown') — active vs passive agency.
9. נִטְבְּעוּ (nitbe'u — 'were sunk') — Red Sea verb (Ex 15:4) vs Greek διεφθάρη ('destroyed').
10. בְּאֵרוֹת (be'erot — 'wells') — patriarchal vocabulary vs Greek ποταμοί ('rivers').
11. תּוֹלַעַת (tola'at — 'Worm') vs Greek Ἄψινθος ('Wormwood') — entirely different names.
12. נִלְקָה (nilqah — 'was eclipsed') — technical astronomical Hebrew vs Greek ἐπλήγη ('struck').
13. רֹחֵף (rochef — 'hovering') — Genesis 1:2 creation verb vs Greek πετωμένου ('flying').
14. Aramaic חֲדָא (chada — 'one') — bilingual code-switching impossible in back-translation.
15. קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'thunderings') — Exodus plague vocabulary (Ex 9:23) setting up the plague sequence.

EXODUS PLAGUE PARALLELS: The four shofar judgments replay the Exodus plagues in sequence: (1) hail and fire (7th plague, Ex 9:23-24), (2) water→blood (1st plague, Ex 7:20), (3) bitter water (Marah, Ex 15:23), (4) darkness (9th plague, Ex 10:21-23). The Hebrew vocabulary in each case uses the Exodus terminology directly.

YOM KIPPUR CEREMONY: Verses 3-5 reproduce the Day of Atonement ritual with exact Levitical vocabulary: the fire-pan (machtah, Lev 16:12), incense (qetoret), the sanctuary (heikhal), smoke ascending before YHWH. The priestly intercession precedes the judgments — the prayers of the holy ones are offered before the plagues are poured out.

JERICHO PATTERN: Seven shopharot, seven messengers, sequential blasting — directly mirroring Joshua 6:4 (seven priests with seven shopharot of jubilee). The walls of the old world are breached as Jericho's walls fell.

CREATION UNDONE: The chapter systematically reverses Genesis 1 — earth struck (v7), sea struck (vv.8-9), fresh water struck (vv.10-11), luminaries struck (v12) — moving backwards through the days of creation. The messenger who witnesses this uses the Genesis 1:2 hovering verb (rachaf), closing the circle. What began with the Spirit hovering over the deep ends with a messenger hovering over the ruins.
